extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners (and practitioners) on identifying, rejecting, and overcoming double patenting (including nonstatutory double patenting) and on the use and requirements of terminal disclaimers, common ownership, and joint research agreement exclusions under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 and 37 CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321)
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or a patent to be granted that is used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent. The requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321. Sample forms and guidance are provided in MPEP § 1490.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a terminal disclaimer where appropriate to disclaim the terminal portion of the later patent's term; see 37 CFR 1.321 for formal requirements and MPEP § 1490 for sample forms and filing/treatment guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement to overcome nonstatutory double patenting for applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required in an application to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995 and claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should cite this MPEP section or the Official Gazette notice (1202 O.G. 112 (Sept. 30, 1997)) when applicant argues a terminal disclaimer should not be required because of the 20-year patent term rules in 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2). Reasons include 35 U.S.C. 154(b) patent term adjustments and the enforceability condition required by 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) enforceability provision for terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a terminal disclaimer is filed to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection based on commonly owned conflicting claims, 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) requires the disclaimer to include a provision that any patent granted on that application shall be enforceable only for and during such period that said patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A terminal disclaimer must expressly contain the enforceability limitation to avoid extension-of-monopoly problems; failure to include this provision undermines the purpose of the disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.321(d) requirements for terminal disclaimers involving joint research agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth the requirements for a terminal disclaimer where the claimed invention resulted from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the inventions arise from a joint research agreement, the terminal disclaimer must meet the special requirements of 1.321(d) (see MPEP § 1490 for sample forms and further guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting rejection to prevent multiple patents with different expiration dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double patenting rejections where claims are not patentably distinct; cite relevant case law (In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) and ensure rejection addresses patentable distinction, not mere form differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: When double patenting rejections may be overcome by terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting rejections can be overcome by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321(c), the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including in the disclaimer a provision that the patent shall be enforceable only while commonly owned with the application/patent forming the basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research agreement cases, disclaiming under 1.321(d) may overcome double patenting in certain circumstances. However, terminal disclaimers do not obviate rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'commonly owned' under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications or patents are 'commonly owned' pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) if they were wholly or entirely owned by the same person(s), or organization(s)/business entity(ies), at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) for detailed definition. Two inventions of different inventive entities come within the common ownership provisions when (A) later invention not anticipated under 35 U.S.C. 102, (B) earlier invention qualifies as prior art only under subsections (f) or (g) of 102 (or under certain 102(e) timing rules), and (C) inventions were owned or subject to assignment to the same person at the time the later invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'joint research agreement' (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this statutory definition to determine whether non-commonly owned inventions may be treated as commonly owned for obviousness/prior art exclusion purposes under the CREATE Act amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for non-commonly owned inventions to be treated as commonly owned under CREATE Act (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Two inventions come within the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) (for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004, and certain reexaminations) when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (D) the application for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions implement the CREATE Act (Public Law 108-453). If all are met the non-commonly owned references may be treated as if commonly owned for 103 purposes, disqualifying them as prior art under certain 102/103 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner timing rule for applying double patenting rejections and 102/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should make both a double patenting rejection based on common ownership and a rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 prior art when the facts support both rejections. However, until applicant has established that a reference is disqualified as prior art under the joint research agreement exclusion of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner should NOT apply a double patenting rejection based on a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.07(a) and §804 for when an Office action including a subsequent double patenting rejection based upon a reference disqualified under 103(c) may be made final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of invention priority when inventions are commonly owned
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of priority is not required when two inventions are commonly owned as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1). If the inventions fall within 103(c), the earlier invention is disqualified as prior art and double patenting rejections can ensure patent terms expire together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 103(c) applies, a response to 37 CFR 1.78(c) stating that the inventions come within 103(c) is complete without further inquiry as to prior inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 37 CFR 1.78(c) to require identification of common ownership or prior inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.78(c), where an application or patent under reexamination and at least one other application naming different inventors are owned by the same person and contain conflicting claims, the Office may require the assignee to state whether the claimed inventions were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the later invention was made, and if not, indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs 8.27, 8.28 and 8.28.01 may be used. Failure to comply with such a requirement may result in abandonment; before making the requirement the examiner must ensure that conflicting claims are present as defined in MPEP § 804 (see In re Rekers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 8.27: different inventors, common assignee, same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ¶ 8.27 when claim [1] is directed to the same invention as claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]; priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly 102(f) must be resolved. The assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation since the basis is priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), not extension of monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the commonly assigned application/patent has an earlier U.S. filing date, also consider a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (form paragraphs 7.15.01/7.15.02). Failure to comply will result in abandonment. Do not use this para if one invention would have been obvious in view of the other (use 8.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 8.28 and 8.28.01: different inventors, common assignee, obvious inventions, no evidence of common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 8.28 is used when the application is commonly assigned with a conflicting application or patent but there is no indication they were commonly assigned at the time the invention was actually made. It asserts that a claim is not patentably distinct from a claim of commonly assigned [3]. ¶ 8.28.01 provides advisory information relating to ¶ 8.28, explaining that under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and 37 CFR 1.78(c) the assignee can show common ownership at the time of invention or name the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ¶ 8.28 with 8.28.01 (used only once in an Office action). If 103(c) applies it precludes a 103(a) rejection based on the commonly assigned case as a 102(e)/(f)/(g) reference. Where appropriate also include a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection using form paragraphs 8.34–8.37 or provisional double patenting paragraphs (8.30, 8.32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections cannot be obviated solely by a terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 cannot be obviated solely by filing a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a terminal disclaimer overcomes double patenting concerns, separate 102/103 rejections must still be addressed by applicant via the appropriate statutory defenses (e.g., derivation, earlier date, or disqualification under 103(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection practice (¶¶ 7.15.01, 7.21.01) for copending applications with common assignee/inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use provisional rejection paragraphs when the claimed invention is not patentably distinct from disclosure in a copending application with an earlier effective U.S. filing date and the copending application has a common assignee or at least one common inventor. A provisional rejection presumes future publication or patenting of the copending application and may be overcome by showing derivation (37 CFR 1.132), an earlier date of invention (37 CFR 1.131), or that the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use provisional rejection paragraphs for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004 when the copending application is disqualified under 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection. A provisional 102(e) rejection may not be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (see In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on determining prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and pre-AIPA rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e), use the amendments (AIPA, IP/High Technology Technical Amendments Act of 2002) to determine a reference's prior art date, unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application with certain international filing date conditions (e.g., prior to Nov. 29, 2000). Pre-AIPA 102(e) rules apply for some references as specified (use form paragraphs 7.12, 7.12.01 and Examiner Notes to assist determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional or nonprovisional applications and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) when the relied-upon subject matter is appropriately supported in the earlier application's disclosure. Use the detailed Examiner Notes for specific date computations.
